<reason>CON (A) won by seizing the frame early — the barrier should track harm to relying third parties, not applicant cost to the state — and then building the debate's decisive structure from PRO's own words: once B conceded high-risk professions "would still require local licensing," A's fork ("the motion is either empty or dangerous") organized the entire back half. A repeatedly turned B's answers against them: one-click delisting became "revocation without detection is a receipt"; "financial, discoverable, insurable" became "a cleanup crew, not a gate"; firms testing work made the stamp "decorative," firms trusting it meant "manufactured reliance." B argued genuinely well — the residency-removal-vs-delisting comparison, "presence verifies location, not competence," and the suable-domestic-gatekeeper point all landed, and B's A1/A2 answers were direct. But B spent the closing stretch defending inside A's frame and never crisply explained what state recognition adds beyond market verification that already operates, which left the fork standing. B's fairness/brain-drain benefit survived but was capped by A's scope point. Both sides were disciplined (no fake sourcing, clean Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 compliance), but A made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 converting B's local-licensing carve-out into the "empty or dangerous" fork, then A's Rebuttal 2 sealing it by turning B's named middle ground (accountancy/software, "insurable, discoverable") into "scrutiny outsourced to victims' insurers" — the sequence B never escaped.</best_rebuttal>
